name: Pomp and Circumstance
description:
There is always more to a musician than just their music. 
This talk uncovers the life of Harikeshanallur Dr. L. Muthiah Bhagavatar (1877–1945), a flamboyant and larger-than-life figure who found joy in every form of expression available to him. He was a renowned musician, a prolific composer, a consummate Harikatha performer, a well-regarded teacher, and the author of a treatise on Carnatic music theory. 
Trained first as a Carnatic musician, Bhagavatar soon turned to Harikatha, finding in its blend of storytelling, song, and stagecraft a fuller outlet for his gifts, quickly becoming one of its most popular exponents. As an important figure at the Mysore court, under the patronage of King Krishnaraja Wodeyar, he composed one hundred and eight songs in praise of Goddess Chamundi, each one a fresh attempt at devotion. At the invitation of Maharani Sethu Parvathy Bai, he later moved to the Travancore Palace, where he became the first principal of the Trivandrum Music College, turning his private joy in music into a public institution for teaching it. 
Even scholarship, for Bhagavatar, became another register of expression. He was the first musician to be awarded a doctorate, for his thesis, Sangita Kalpadrumam. Published only after his death, his theoretical work was born of the same curiosity that drove his performances. Across his lifetime he composed more than four hundred songs in multiple languages and introduced around twenty new ragas into the Carnatic tradition. In 1920, he founded a gurukula, the Tyagaraja Sangita Vidyalaya, in Madurai, ensuring that this capacity for joyful reinvention would outlive him, carried forward by students such as Madurai Mani Iyer.

name: The Unknown Mahatmas Who Made the Mahatma
description:
We know the freedom struggle’s great names, its fighters, and its stars. But there are many more influences that often get lost in the stories. This performance traces the people Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi met along his journey: the lesser-known encounters, quiet and easily overlooked, who helped turn him into the great man history remembers. 
Through song, anecdote, and lore, the performance unpacks the word itself. Mahatma. It asks what this title might still mean today, in a world so far removed from the one that first gave it to him. What does it really take to turn a man into a Mahatma? 


The Lesser-Known Figures in Gandhi’s Journey

name: Gombe
description:
This evening brings together three short films, followed by a conversation between filmmakers Hansa Thapliyal and Paromita Vohra. Each film turns an intimate lens on questions of art, choice, and connection. 
The Outside In
25m 03s | 2019 | English, Marathi with English Subtitles
Two dollmakers, working with simple, discarded materials, gently loosen our resistance to empathy. The film collaborates with them and their dolls, blurring the line between what lies outside us and within. 
Kya Hai Ye Samjhauta
9m | 2024 | Hindi with English Subtitles
Born from twelve caseworkers’ recordings across rural Uttar Pradesh, this film uses scraps of cloth, needle and thread, and the timbre of human voices to explore women’s choices in the face of domestic violence. This film looks at the word samjhauta and asks: do you make your terms? 
Duniya Kee Raunak
19m 40s | 2026 | Telugu, Marathi, Hindi with English Subtitles
Must a television screen decide what our lives will be like? Little Mansoor steps beyond his window to befriend the world outside. Blending shadow puppetry, theatre, and stop motion, the film is a tribute to the earliest, most playful histories of cinema. 
Please Note: Children under 16 are to be accompanied by an adult.

name: Beyond the Buzz
description:
This panel discussion examines India’s relationship with alcohol, from the colonial history to the current how deeply that marketing is rooted in history. Panelists will trace how colonial rule promoted distillery-based alcohol production to extract revenue for the empire, and how those same patterns continue to shape how alcohol is sold and consumed today. What does a drink marketed as celebration, sophistication, even heart health, carry behind the glamour? 
Though direct advertising is banned in India, the liquor industry remains worth an estimated sixty-five billion dollars, sustained instead through aspiration, imagery, and social pressure. Recent research suggests that between twenty-five and forty percent of Indian drinkers qualify as hazardous or dependent drinkers, a gap the panel will contextualise through the lived and professional experience of its speakers, who bring perspectives as mental health practitioners and individuals with firsthand experience of addiction. Changing the image of alcohol as an essential ingredient of celebration, the panel argues, may be one of the most consequential shifts available to public health today.

name: The Many Pasts of Panipat, 1761
description:
A great “what if?” moment in Indian history, the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761 has produced martyrs, ballads, and endless partisan debate. This lecture examines how its retelling, across school textbooks, Hindu nationalist historiography, and cinema, has flattened a complex event into a tale of heroes and villains. It raises the question, whose Panipat are we really remembering? 
The vernacular primary sources tell a different story: where popular memory insists on certainty, they equivocate, contradict, and complicate. A micro history of the battle reveals multiple pasts, remembered and recorded by multiple men. This lecture makes a case for why critical historians cannot ignore this plurality while narrating the event to a generation raised on a communal rendering of Indian history. 
About Satish Chandra 
Professor Satish Chandra (1922-2017) was one of India’s foremost historians and a towering authority on medieval Indian history. Over a distinguished four-decade career, he taught at leading universities across the country, including Allahabad University, Aligarh Muslim University, Delhi University, Rajasthan University, and finally Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU). At JNU, he co-founded the Centre for Historical Studies alongside S. Gopal, Bipin Chandra, and Romila Thapar. As Chairman of the University Grants Commission, he went on to help shape academic life across India, and in 1985, deeply committed to intellectual exchange, he co-founded the Society for Indian Ocean Studies. A thoughtful historian who brought a Marxist approach to the field, Chandra’s work bridged eras and ideas, leaving an enduring mark on the study of India’s past.

name: Salaki Suthrada Bombe
description:
Wooden figures dressed in Moodalapaaya finery, come alive on rods and strings. This performance brings traditional folk puppets to the stage, performed by a troupe carrying the craft forward across five generations. 
Each puppet stands three to three and a half feet tall, carved by hand and strung with iron rods and thread for manipulation, a technique passed down through a family of performers for nearly a century and a half. The evening opens with the history of the form and its place within Karnataka’s wider puppetry traditions, before the artists demonstrate how a puppet is carved, dressed, and strung. Audience members are then invited to try the rods and strings themselves, before the evening closes with a full performance drawn from Karnataka’s mythological and folk repertoire. 
This performance is the ninth edition of the BIC Jaanapada series. 
BIC Jaanapada is a series, programmed every two months, celebrating Karnataka’s folk traditions through the lens of regional identity and cultural preservation. Curated in collaboration with Tvarita Arts Collective India, the program combines scholarly discourse with live performances to explore the deep connections between geography and artistic expression. Through demonstrations, performances, and academic discussions, each session examines how landscape and local culture have shaped these distinct artistic practices.

name: Evocation
description:
What turns stillness into joy? 
This Hindustani classical concert showcases a selection of ragas chosen for their emotive range, each one a distinct attempt to reach toward the sublime. Across the evening, the mood shifts without warning, from meditative stillness to sudden, unguarded joy. 
These turns arise from within the ragas themselves, each one holding its own energy. The recital rests on technique, emotion, and contemplation in equal measure, offering an audience attuned to the form a close, unhurried encounter with what Hindustani music can carry.

name: Echoes of the Earth
description:
65 min | English with subtitles | India | Ganesh Shankar Raj 
Echoes of the Earth: Indigenous Knowledge and Climate Resilience in Karnataka and Kerala explores how traditional knowledge, shaped by centuries of observation, can build climate resilience and nurture a careful, sustainable relationship with the environment. 
Through personal stories and intimate portraits of everyday life, the film highlights practices that conserve forests, biodiversity and natural resources. It also reflects on how climate change is already affecting plants, wildlife and ecosystems, particularly among the Soliga communities of Karnataka. What can these knowledge systems teach us about living sustainably, and what might be overlooked when their ecological dimensions are viewed mainly through cultural or religious traditions? 
The screening will be followed by a panel discussion on the role of Indigenous women as knowledge holders and contributors to environmental stewardship. Indigenous knowledge is not only a legacy of the past, but a living resource for building climate resilience today.

name: Little Language Film Festival
description:
Languages carry more than words. They hold songs, stories, myths, proverbs, poetry and the lived experiences of the communities that speak them. This film festival is not, at its heart, simply a celebration of linguistic diversity. It is a reminder of what is at stake when a language disappears: an entire perspective and expression of the world. 
Across India, languages such as Tiwa, Kodava, Santhali, Kurmali, Kokborok and Sherdukpen are spoken by communities whose linguistic traditions are increasingly vulnerable. Globalisation and the dominance of economically powerful languages have accelerated this process, putting many lesser-spoken languages at risk of disappearing. This film festival brings together films in some of these near-forgotten languages, offering an opportunity to encounter their speakers, stories and worlds on their own terms. 
Alongside the screenings, the festival will bring together filmmakers, writers and others working with endangered languages for a conversation on the importance of endangered languages. 
Schedule 
Day 1 | Oct 10 | 11:30am – 5:30pm 
11:30am – 11:45am: Opening Note 
11:45am – 1:30pm: Sikaisal / If Only Trees Could Talk
104 minutes | Tiwa with English subtitles | 2022 | Bobby Sarma Baruah
Sikaisal won the NFA for Best Film in Tiwa language. Directed by Bobby Sarma Baruah, it is Based on the real-life struggles of Maheswar Patar, a dedicated school teacher in Ulukunchi village of Assam. Highlighting his determination to educate children in a remote community of Northeast India in the face of numerous challenges, the film won a Special Jury Mention at the 28th Kolkata International Film Festival. 
1:30pm – 3pm: Break 
3pm – 5:30pm: Kherwal
125 minutes | Santali with English subtitles | 2023 | Uttam Kamati
Kherwal is an acclaimed Santali-language film written, directed and produced by Uttam Kamati. After the sudden death of the Norwegian Samuel, an academic Padre who was researching their tribal culture, Bidu strives to fulfill the Padre’s last wish: to be buried in the village. This sets off a poignant journey for Bidu’s young son, who is devastated as he wanted to travel to Norway with the academic. Kherwal uniquely features non-professional actors, including a local mobile repair shop owner as the lead character. The film has been celebrated on the festival circuit, winning awards at the Jaipur IFF and the IFF of Kerala. 
The screening will be followed by an audience Q&A. 
Day 2 | Oct 11 | 11:30am – 7pm 
11:30am – 1pm: Panel discussion on Endangered Languages
A conversation on the importance of endangered languages and the cultural worlds they hold. Filmmakers, writers and practitioners reflect on the challenges faced by lesser-spoken languages, and the ways in which they can be documented, nurtured and kept alive. 
1pm – 2pm: Break 
2pm – 4:30pm: Ber / The Root
125 minutes | Kodava with English subtitles | 2023 | Prakash Kariappa
Ber was written, directed and produced by ex-service man Prakash Kariappa. The Kodava language film encapsulates the intricacies of a father-daughter relationship and in the process delves into themes of tradition, generational divides, and the need to preserve the Kodava culture. It has featured in festivals including BIFFes and Dhaka International Film Festival. 
The screening will be followed by an audience Q&A. 
4:30pm – 4:45pm: Tea Break 
4:45pm – 6:30pm: Whispers Of The Mountains
90 minutes | Rajasthani with English subtitles | 2025 | Jigar Nagda
Whispers Of The Mountains is a Rajasthani language drama directed by Jigar Nagda, featured in the Indian Panorama section of the 56th IFFI at Goa. It explores the fragile balance between ecological preservation and the livelihoods of communities living in the Aravalli region, underscoring the human cost of mining in Northwest India. 
The screening will be followed by an audience Q&A. 
6:30pm – 7pm: Closing Note

name: The Belle of Amherst
description:
The Belle of Amherst by William Luce, written in 1976, is a play based on the life of American poet Emily Dickinson. It was first performed by Julie Harris, who won a Tony for her role, in 1977. The story, narrated by the eccentric Emily herself, liberally interspersed with her sublime poetry, is a truly soulful journey for both the character and her audience. Susan George will do a dramatised reading of the play. 
Image Credit
The portrait of Emily Dickinson is from the only currently authenticated photograph, a daguerreotype ca. 1847 in the Amherst College Archives & Special Collections.

name: Moksha Mudra
description:
This Bharatanatyam production traces the parallel cycles of women and the earth, each unfolding through the turn of the seasons. As the earth moves through its changing forms, its female protagonists move through their own inner seasons, carrying turmoil that mirrors the natural world around them before dissolving into liberation. 
Through evocative movement, music, and storytelling, the work moves between distinct narratives: the grace of Amrapali, the devotion of Radha, the resilience of Sita, the courage of Rani Lakshmibai, and the environmental legacy of Amrita Devi. Each episode draws out a different facet of feminine strength and transformation, building toward a single, layered portrait of endurance across time.

This interactive storytelling session takes us back to the childhood of Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi. From his hometown to his school days, the session is filled with songs, drama, and adventure. There is power in speaking the truth, and together, we shall find it! 



Around the World in 50 Sundays is a journey that begins, not with a ticket, but with opening a book. In a city like Bangalore where families are always in motion, the BIC Library hopes to offer stillness and a quiet, welcoming space for both parents and children where reading becomes a shared experience. Every Sunday, we open our doors to invite you into a library that listens; building a rhythm of return, a habit of joy and a new community bound not just by books, but by the weekly ritual of reading together.  
We welcome your ideas and input. If you have suggestions for children’s events or activities that align with this vision, we’d love to hear from you. Please reach out to us at library@bangaloreinternationalcentre.org
